title: Does Low Unemployment Cause Inflation? The Phillips Curve, Tested
description:
For decades, economists believed you could have low unemployment or low inflation, but not both. We test that idea, the Phillips curve, with a simple model on more than sixty years of official US data, decade by decade.

Every number and every fitted line is computed from public data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, via FRED. The sources are listed below.

claims.says: In the 1960s, lower unemployment went with higher inflation
In the 1960s a straight line explained most of inflation's ups and downs
From 1970 to 1985 the line explained almost nothing
Inflation in the 1970s and early 1980s reached more than double its 1960s peak
From 1986 to 2019 the relationship was very weak
Since 2020, low unemployment has again tended to go with higher inflation
Over the whole period since 1960, there is no clear line

scenes.narration: When unemployment is very low, do prices start to rise faster? It is one of the most important questions in economics, because central banks act on the answer. If low unemployment really pushes up inflation, then a central bank fighting inflation may have to accept more people out of work. Today we will test that idea with more than sixty years of official data and a simple model, decade by decade. The answer turns out to be more interesting than a yes or a no.

First, the two lines we will compare. This is the unemployment rate, the share of people who want a job and are looking for one, but do not have one. It rises sharply in every recession and falls slowly in good times. The latest reading is {{ latest(unemp) | num }} percent. Since 1960 it has been as low as {{ lowest(unemp, "1960", "latest") | num }} percent and as high as {{ highest(unemp, "1960", "latest") | num }} percent.

And this is inflation, measured as how much consumer prices rose compared with the same month a year earlier. You can see the great inflation of the 1970s, peaking at {{ highest(infl, "1970", "1985") | pct1 }} in {{ year_of_highest(infl, "1970", "1985") | year }}, the long calm period after that, and the sudden jump after the pandemic. The latest reading is {{ latest(infl) | pct1 }}.

chart.title: Inflation
chart.subtitle: Change in consumer prices on a year earlier

scenes.narration: In 1958, an economist named Bill Phillips noticed something in old British data. When unemployment was low, wages rose fast. When unemployment was high, wages barely moved. The idea makes sense. When workers are scarce, employers compete for them, pay rises, and businesses pass the cost on in their prices. American economists turned this into a simple trade-off between unemployment and inflation. It became known as the Phillips curve.

chart.title: The idea: scarce workers push prices up
chart.label: THE PHILLIPS CURVE

scenes.narration: Here is the 1960s. Each dot is one year. Across is the average unemployment rate that year, and up is inflation. Watch the dots appear in order. Now we fit a straight line through them with a simple regression. The shaded band shows how uncertain that line is. The pattern is striking. Lower unemployment went with higher inflation. Each extra point of unemployment came with about {{ 0 - slope(unemp, infl, "1960", "1969") * 100 | pts }} less inflation, and the line explains about {{ r_squared(unemp, infl, "1960", "1969") | pct }} of the ups and downs. No wonder economists believed it.

chart.title: The 1960s: a clean trade-off
chart.subtitle: One dot per year, with a fitted straight line

scenes.narration: Then came the 1970s and early 1980s. Oil shocks hit, and something the theory said should not happen did happen. Unemployment and inflation rose together. Economists called it stagflation. Inflation reached more than double its 1960s peak, while unemployment was high too. Fit the same straight line now, and it explains about {{ r_squared(unemp, infl, "1970", "1985") | pct }} of the movement. Practically nothing. The neat curve had broken.

chart.title: 1970 to 1985: the curve breaks
chart.subtitle: One dot per year, with a fitted straight line

scenes.narration: What went wrong? The best explanation is expectations. Once people expect high inflation, they ask for bigger raises and businesses raise prices in advance, whatever unemployment is doing. After the Federal Reserve crushed inflation in the early 1980s, people came to expect low and steady inflation again. And then the opposite puzzle appeared. From 1986 to 2019, unemployment swung from high to very low, but inflation barely reacted. The fitted line is almost flat, and it explains only {{ r_squared(unemp, infl, "1986", "2019") | pct }} of the movement.

chart.title: 1986 to 2019: a flat line
chart.subtitle: One dot per year, with a fitted straight line

scenes.narration: Then the pandemic. Unemployment shot up in 2020 and fell back fast. As it fell, and with supply chains broken and lots of spending, inflation jumped to {{ highest(infl, "2020", "latest") | pct1 }}. Join the years in order and you can see a loop rather than a line. Since 2020, lower unemployment has once again tended to go with higher inflation, but with only a handful of years, it is far too early to say the old curve is back.

chart.title: Since 2019: a loop
chart.subtitle: One dot per year, joined in order

scenes.narration: So, does low unemployment cause inflation? Sometimes, a little, but not reliably. Over the whole period since 1960, one straight line explains about {{ r_squared(unemp, infl, "1960", "latest") | pct }} of the movement. The relationship is real in some decades and almost invisible in others, because what people expect inflation to be matters as much as how many people have a job. That is why central banks watch expectations so closely.

chart.title: Sometimes. It depends on what people expect.
chart.label: THE ANSWER

scenes.narration: A note on the model. A fitted line shows that two things moved together. It does not prove that one caused the other, and yearly averages hide a lot of detail. Economists use richer models, with expectations, oil prices and slack in the economy. But even this simple version tells the main story of sixty years of economic history in four pictures.

chart.title: Moving together is not the same as causing
chart.label: A NOTE ON THE MODEL
